bill.title: A bill to ensure the fairness, transparency, and consistency of disqualifying provisions administered by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission and the Securities and Exchange Commission, and for other purposes.
bill.latestActionText: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.

industries.rationale: The bill directly affects how financial firms and professionals regulated by the SEC and CFTC are disqualified from certain activities and how they may seek waivers.
Digital asset firms subject to CFTC oversight would be affected by changes to disqualification and waiver procedures.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would standardize the rules used by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission and the Securities and Exchange Commission when they disqualify individuals or firms from certain privileges due to past misconduct. It aims to make these disqualification processes more consistent and transparent across both agencies. The bill addresses how the two regulators handle waivers and exemptions from automatic disqualifications.

bill.title: Fair Access to Banking Act
bill.latestActionText: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.

industries.rationale: The bill directly regulates how banks and credit unions may deny financial services to customers.
Digital asset firms have frequently reported being denied banking services, making them likely beneficiaries of fair-access requirements.
Firearms businesses have reported service denials from banks citing reputational risk, which this bill would prohibit.
Cannabis and related businesses have faced banking access challenges that this bill's requirements could address.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would restrict banks, credit unions, and payment card networks from refusing service to customers who comply with the law. Financial institutions could only deny service based on documented, quantitative risk standards set in advance, and could not cite reputational concerns as a reason. Violations would trigger penalties including loss of federal deposit insurance, exclusion from electronic payment systems, and potential civil lawsuits by affected customers.

plain.whoItTouches: Anyone with a bank account, a loan or savings.

bill.title: FIND Act
bill.latestActionText: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.

industries.rationale: The bill directly protects firearm manufacturers, dealers, and trade associations from discrimination in federal contracting.
Banks and financial institutions that provide services to federal contractors would be affected if they maintain policies restricting business with firearm entities.
Defense contractors frequently hold federal contracts and may need to review policies regarding firearm-related business relationships.
Insurance companies that contract with the federal government would need to ensure their underwriting policies do not discriminate against firearm businesses.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would prohibit federal agencies from awarding contracts to companies that discriminate against firearm manufacturers, dealers, or trade associations. Contractors would be required to certify they have no policies that discriminate against firearm-related businesses and will not adopt such policies during the contract term. The requirement would apply to both prime contractors and subcontractors, with penalties for violations, but would not apply to sole-source contracts.

plain.whoItTouches: People who own or buy guns.

bill.title: CARE Act of 2025
bill.latestActionText: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance. (Sponsor introductory remarks on measure: CR S7964)

industries.rationale: The bill creates a new Medicare payment stream for ground ambulance services that do not result in transport, directly affecting ambulance operators' revenues and service models.
Medicare payment policy changes for emergency medical services affect the program's costs and may influence private insurers' coverage decisions for similar services.

bill.plainSummary: This bill directs Medicare to test a five-year program that would pay ambulance services even when they respond to an emergency call but do not transport the patient to a hospital. Payment rates would generally match what Medicare currently pays when a patient is transported. The Government Accountability Office would study how the program affects Medicare beneficiaries' access to emergency medical services and their health outcomes.

plain.whoItTouches: Anyone who sees a doctor or pays for care.

bill.title: A bill to establish consumer transparency and protection requirements for artificial intelligence chatbots, and for other purposes.
bill.latestActionText: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

industries.rationale: The bill directly regulates AI chatbot operators, imposing new disclosure and transparency obligations on software and internet platform companies that deploy these systems.
Retailers and e-commerce platforms that use AI chatbots for customer service would face new compliance requirements for disclosing automated interactions.
Banks and financial services firms that deploy AI chatbots for customer support or account services would need to meet the new transparency standards.
Telecom and cable providers that use AI chatbots for customer service interactions would be subject to the disclosure requirements.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would require companies that operate AI chatbots to disclose to users when they are interacting with artificial intelligence rather than a human. It would establish transparency requirements so consumers know they are communicating with an automated system. The bill would also create consumer protection standards for how AI chatbots operate and interact with the public.

bill.title: National Plan for Epilepsy Act
bill.latestActionText: Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions. Ordered to be reported with an amendment in the nature of a substitute favorably.

industries.rationale: The bill's focus on epilepsy treatment, diagnosis, and cure research directly affects pharmaceutical and medical device companies developing epilepsy therapies.
The national plan's coordination of epilepsy care and services would affect hospitals and health systems that diagnose and treat epilepsy patients.

bill.plainSummary: This bill directs the Department of Health and Human Services to create and carry out a national plan to address epilepsy, including prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and research coordination across federal agencies. HHS must establish an advisory council that reports to Congress every two years and must itself submit annual progress reports with recommended actions. These requirements would remain in effect until the end of 2035.

bill.latestActionText: Indefinitely postponed by Senate by Unanimous Consent.

industries.rationale: The bill would eliminate a fee charged to oil and gas companies for methane emissions above specified thresholds.

That rule established procedures for charging oil and gas companies an annual fee when their methane and other greenhouse gas emissions exceed certain thresholds. If enacted, the resolution would eliminate these compliance requirements and the associated emissions charge program.

subjects: Hybrid, electric, and advanced technology vehicles

industries.rationale: Automotive manufacturers would face different regulatory obligations depending on whether California's distinct emission standards remain in effect.
The Advanced Clean Cars II regulations affect the market for electric vehicle charging infrastructure and clean-energy vehicle adoption.
Electric utilities face demand changes tied to electric vehicle adoption rates influenced by state emission standards.
Petroleum refiners and distributors face market impacts from regulations that affect the mix of gasoline versus electric vehicles sold.

bill.title: A joint resolution providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Department of Energy relating to "Energy Conservation Program: Energy Conservation Standards for Consumer Gas-fired Instantaneous Water Heaters".
bill.latestActionText: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 12.

industries.rationale: Manufacturers of gas-fired instantaneous water heaters would be directly affected by the nullification of energy efficiency standards that govern their product design and compliance costs.
Natural gas suppliers have a stake in standards that affect the efficiency and market competitiveness of gas-fired appliances versus electric alternatives.
Energy efficiency standards for gas appliances can influence the relative market share of gas versus electric water heating systems.
Contractors and builders who install water heaters would face different product availability and compliance requirements depending on whether the standards remain in effect.

bill.plainSummary: This joint resolution would overturn a Department of Energy rule issued in December 2024 that set new energy efficiency standards for gas-fired instantaneous water heaters (commonly called tankless water heaters). The DOE rule required these appliances to meet stricter energy conservation requirements. If this resolution passes, the new standards would be nullified and would not take effect.

bill.latestActionText: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.

industries.rationale: The resolution directly affects heavy-duty vehicle manufacturers, trucking companies, and motor carriers by determining whether they must comply with California's stricter emission standards.
Automotive and engine manufacturers would face different regulatory requirements depending on whether California's waiver stands or is nullified.
Zero-emission vehicle mandates affect demand for electric vehicle charging infrastructure and clean energy services for commercial fleets.
Requirements for zero-emission trucks and airport shuttles would influence electricity demand and infrastructure investment for fleet charging.

bill.plainSummary: This resolution would block an Environmental Protection Agency decision that allowed California to enforce its own stricter emission standards for heavy-duty trucks and engines. The EPA had granted California a waiver from federal preemption rules, permitting the state to require cleaner trucks, zero-emission airport shuttles, and advanced clean truck standards. If passed, the resolution would nullify that waiver and prevent California from implementing these regulations.

bill.title: HALT Fentanyl Act

industries.rationale: The bill changes registration and licensing requirements for pharmaceutical researchers conducting controlled substance research and affects the regulatory classification of chemical substances.
The bill establishes new criminal penalties and quantity thresholds that will affect prosecution and defense of drug trafficking cases.
Universities and research institutions conducting controlled substance research would be subject to the new registration processes and requirements established by the bill.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would permanently classify all fentanyl-related substances as Schedule I controlled substances, meaning they would be treated as having high abuse potential and no accepted medical use. It sets the same criminal penalties and quantity thresholds for fentanyl-related substances as currently apply to fentanyl analogues. The bill also creates a streamlined registration process for researchers studying Schedule I substances and relaxes some requirements for research facilities working with controlled substances.

plain.whoItTouches: People caught up in the criminal law, and victims of crime.

bill.latestActionText: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.
subjects: Hybrid, electric, and advanced technology vehicles

industries.rationale: The bill directly affects heavy-duty trucking by determining whether stricter California emission standards apply to commercial vehicles and engines.
The bill affects manufacturers of heavy-duty vehicles and engines by determining whether they must comply with California's stricter NOx emission requirements.
Stricter emission standards for heavy-duty vehicles could affect demand for diesel fuel and related petroleum products.

bill.plainSummary: This joint resolution would overturn an Environmental Protection Agency decision that allowed California to enforce stricter pollution standards for heavy-duty trucks and engines than federal law normally permits. The EPA had granted California a waiver to implement its "Omnibus Low NOx" regulation, which sets tougher limits on nitrogen oxide emissions from vehicles. If this resolution passes, that waiver would be nullified and California would be blocked from enforcing those stricter standards.
